draft.title: Arguments and evidence
card: An argument is a reason a writer gives to support their contention. A writer usually gives several arguments, each with its own point.
Evidence is what a writer uses to back up an argument. It shows readers that the reason is not just an opinion.
numbers or figures, such as the percentage of students who walk to school.
an expert view is a claim from a person with special knowledge, such as a doctor. An example is a real case that shows the point in action.
draft.remember: An argument is a reason for the contention. Evidence is what backs that reason up.

a.q: A writer says schools should start later. One reason is that teenagers learn better when well rested. What is this reason?
opts: An argument that supports the contention
The evidence that backs up the contention
The issue that people disagree on
A statistic that backs up the contention
a.why: The reason is an argument because it explains why the contention is right. It is not evidence yet, as nothing has been given to back it up. It also has no figures, so it is not a statistic.
a.clue: It is a reason, not proof that the reason is true.

b.q: Ravi argues that cities need more bike lanes. To back this up, he reports that a transport researcher studied city streets and found fewer cyclist injuries where lanes were separated from traffic. What kind of evidence is this?
b.why: The claim comes from a researcher, a person with special knowledge, so it is an expert view. It is not a statistic because it gives no figures. It is not a personal example because it does not describe one real case.
b.clue: Look at who the claim comes from, and check whether any figures are given.

a.best: An argument that supports the contention
